subject: Biology
title: Gene Therapy
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Gene Therapy.

hook.text: Gene therapy aims to fix diseases by replacing or repairing faulty genes inside a patient's cells.

buildup.text: A harmless virus is often used as a delivery vehicle to carry the corrected gene into cells.

discovery.text: In 2017, gene therapy cured a form of inherited blindness by delivering a working gene to the retina.

twist.text: Early trials in the 1990s had tragic setbacks. One patient died from an immune reaction.

climax.text: Today, approved gene therapies treat blood disorders, blindness, and certain cancers.

punchline.text: Fix the gene, fix the disease.

quiz.question: How is a corrected gene typically delivered into a patient's cells?
options: Using a harmless virus as a vehicle
By direct injection of raw DNA

details.summary: Gene therapy treats disease by introducing, altering, or replacing genetic material within a patient's cells. Using modified viruses or other delivery systems, functional copies of defective genes can be delivered to restore normal protein production.
details.whyItMatters: Gene therapy offers potential cures for diseases previously considered untreatable. Recent successes in treating blindness, spinal muscular atrophy, and sickle cell disease are transforming lives after decades of research.
takeaways: Viral vectors deliver therapeutic genes into patient cells
Luxturna restores vision in patients with inherited retinal dystrophy
Gene therapy for sickle cell disease has shown remarkable early results

faq.question: How are modified viruses used in gene therapy?
faq.answer: Viruses are natural experts at inserting genetic material into cells. Scientists remove the viral disease-causing genes and replace them with therapeutic genes. The disabled virus infects target cells and delivers the corrective gene without causing illness.

faq.question: Why has gene therapy taken so long to become reality?
faq.answer: Early attempts caused severe immune reactions and even cancer when inserted genes activated oncogenes. Decades of work improved vector safety, targeting precision, and dosing. Modern adeno-associated virus vectors are far safer than early retroviral approaches.
